# Nine Hundred Lines {#sec-nine-hundred-lines}

| Red Penn, my editor at a small press,
| Still emailed me, "Checking in."
| By the month the tool was named, worn thin,
| My answers had run out, I'll confess.

| So, this time, I'd send Red a plan:
| An outline for chapter twelve, which would
| Show him the book still moved, and could
| Show me where to. And I began:

| I typed "Chapter twelve", and sat.
| The README, in the window near,
| Was open. It was usually here.
| It started at a page; and that

| Was on the morning after the name.
| Each evening since, the tool would learn
| Some new thing, and each new thing would earn
| A paragraph. Examples came,

| And sections to explain them: text
| On the config file, and one more,
| Longer, on the second, written for
| The first; it now did not. And next:

| A table of contents. Problems, here,
| Ranked by how much each one shamed me. None
| Of all the things that I had done
| Was longer than this, all that year.

| It had headings. Headings look
| Like progress. The outline? Two words, though,
| And one of them a number. So
| I sent Red the README, and I took

| Three lines above it, saying I'd done
| This for the book. I didn't say
| It was instead. No need: on display,
| Nine hundred lines, and every one.

| I still think it was the best
| I wrote in those three years. It said
| What the tool did, clearly, and, read
| Through, no part of it fought the rest.

| The tool did all the README said.
| I could not, then or to this day,
| Have said as much, in any way,
| Of anything else I'd sent to Red.

| It was documentation, which is my job, which is the problem.

| Red read all of it. I know, since he,
| Months later, writing on something new,
| Quoted, as one who'd read it through,
| Line six hundred and twelve to me.

| That day he wrote back just one line:
| "Is there a chapter in here?"
| I read it all again, the way he'd peer,
| For one, through all its hundreds, all nine.

| There wasn't.
| There was a section called Getting Started.
